rate on clear-*kick* fourth downs was still near zero. Campbell's aggression was aimed at the short-
yardage, middle-of-the-field fourth downs where the math is lopsided, and the two decisions from the
NFC Championship Game that defined his reputation for critics were, by every model, among the *closest*
calls he made. The fair grade is the whole season's ledger, not the two snaps everyone remembers.
:::

## Two-point decisions: down 14, down 8

The two-point decision is the cleanest decision tree in football, because it is one play with two
outcomes and a short future. Since the extra point moved back in 2015, the try has been close to a
coin flip on expected points:

```{python}
#| label: two-point
tries = reg[(reg.two_point_attempt == 1) | (reg.extra_point_attempt == 1)].copy()
tries["two"] = (tries.two_point_attempt == 1).astype(float)
P2 = (tries.loc[tries.two == 1, "two_point_conv_result"] == "success").mean()
PX = (tries.loc[tries.two == 0, "extra_point_result"] == "good").mean()
print(f"2016-2025: two-point tries succeeded {P2:.1%} of the time "
      f"({int(tries.two.sum()):,} tries) = {2 * P2:.2f} points; "
      f"extra points good {PX:.1%} = {PX:.2f} points")
```

When the averages are equal, the score decides, and the most debated score is this one: **you were down
14, you just scored a touchdown, and you are now down 8 before the try.** The traditional move is to kick
(down 7) and plan to kick again after the next touchdown to force overtime. The analytics move is to go
for two now. Here is the whole tree, assuming you score the second touchdown and the opponent doesn't
score again (the only world in which this decision matters), and that overtime is a coin flip.

- **Kick first.** Make it (probability $k$) and you're down 7; after the next touchdown you are down 1,
  and you take the better of kicking for overtime ($k \times \tfrac12$) or going for the win ($p$). Miss
  it, and you're down 8; after the next touchdown you are down 2 and must go for two to reach overtime
  ($p \times \tfrac12$).
- **Go for two first.** Make it (probability $p$) and you're down 6; the next touchdown ties the game and
  the extra point wins it ($k$, or overtime if it misses). Miss it, and you're down 8; after the next
  touchdown you are down 2 and go for two to tie ($p \times \tfrac12$).

$$
W_\text{kick first} = k \cdot \max\!\left(\tfrac{k}{2},\, p\right) + (1-k)\,\tfrac{p}{2}, \qquad
W_\text{go first} = p\left(k + \tfrac{1-k}{2}\right) + (1-p)\,\tfrac{p}{2}
$$

```{python}
#| label: down14
def w_kick_first(p, k=PX, ot=0.5):
    return k * np.maximum(k * ot, p) + (1 - k) * p * ot


def w_go_first(p, k=PX, ot=0.5):
    return p * (k + (1 - k) * ot) + (1 - p) * p * ot


ps = np.linspace(0.25, 0.65, 401)
breakeven_p = ps[np.argmax(w_go_first(ps) > w_kick_first(ps))]
print(f"At p = {P2:.3f}: kick first {w_kick_first(P2):.1%}, go first {w_go_first(P2):.1%}; "
      f"going first is better whenever p > {breakeven_p:.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-down14
#| fig-cap: "Down 14, you score a touchdown: the chance of winning with each plan, assuming you score the second touchdown and stop the opponent (overtime counted as a coin flip, extra points good 94% of the time). Going for two after the first touchdown beats kicking whenever your two-point success rate is above about 35%; at the league's 2016-2025 rate it is worth about 12 extra points of win probability in the games where you score twice. The reason: going early turns the second touchdown into a win (if the first try worked) or tells you in advance that you need two (if it didn't), instead of aiming the whole comeback at overtime."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
ax.plot(ps, w_go_first(ps), color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, label="Go for two after the first TD")
ax.plot(ps, w_kick_first(ps), color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, label="Kick first (then the better choice)")
ax.axvline(P2, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.text(P2 + 0.004, 0.27, f"league 2016-25:\n{pct(P2, 1)}", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
ax.axvline(breakeven_p, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax.text(breakeven_p - 0.004, 0.62, f"break-even\n{pct(breakeven_p)}", fontsize=7.5,
        color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="top")
for f, c, dx, dy, ha, va in [(w_go_first, style.SERIES[0], -0.012, 0.02, "right", "bottom"),
                              (w_kick_first, style.SERIES[1], 0.008, -0.022, "left", "top")]:
    ax.scatter([P2], [f(P2)], s=26, color=c, zorder=4, edgecolor=style.SURFACE)
    ax.text(P2 + dx, f(P2) + dy, pct(f(P2)), fontsize=7.5, color=c, fontweight="bold",
            ha=ha, va=va)
ax.set_xlim(0.25, 0.65)
ax.set_ylim(0.25, 0.72)
fmt = plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}")
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(fmt)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(fmt)
ax.set_xlabel("Your two-point success rate")
ax.set_ylabel("Win probability, given two TDs")
ax.set_title("Down 14: go for two on the first touchdown")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
plt.show()
```

The tree makes the logic visible. Kicking twice aims the entire comeback at overtime, which you win half
the time. Going early gives you a roughly even chance of turning the second touchdown into an outright
win, and when the first try fails you still have the overtime route, just with a two-pointer attached,
and you *know* it while there is still time to plan the last drive. That knowledge is a bonus the formula
doesn't count: a team that knows it needs two scores can play the rest of the game accordingly (going
for it on fourth down, for instance), while the kick-first team learns about a missed extra point too
late to adjust.

Two honest caveats. First, the formula assumes **two more touchdowns and nothing else**. If the
opponent might score again, or you might settle for a field goal, the comparison shifts, and with more
time left the margin will change before it matters, which is why the down-8 case is a fourth-quarter
question. Second, the 50% overtime is a simplification: under the 2025 rule both teams get a possession
in regular-season overtime, and a tie is possible.

The same reasoning settles **down 8** on its own: if you score a touchdown when trailing by 8, you are
down 2 and must go for two to tie; there is no decision at all, which is exactly why the down-14 team
prefers to find out early. Have coaches absorbed this? The data say yes, and quickly.

```{python}
#| label: fig-down8
#| fig-cap: "How often teams went for two when trailing by 8 right after a touchdown (the down-14 situation), 2016-2025 regular seasons, for tries in the fourth quarter and in any quarter. Nobody did it in 2016 or 2017; in 2025 about half of fourth-quarter tries at down 8 were two-point attempts. The samples are small (about 12 to 21 fourth-quarter tries a season), so single seasons bounce around; the trend does not."
d8 = tries[tries.score_differential == -8]
d8_rate = pd.DataFrame({"Fourth quarter": d8[d8.qtr == 4].groupby("season").two.mean(),
                        "Any quarter": d8.groupby("season").two.mean()})
d8_n = d8[d8.qtr == 4].groupby("season").size()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
for k, c in enumerate(d8_rate.columns):
    ax.plot(d8_rate.index, d8_rate[c], color=style.SERIES[k], lw=2, marker="o", ms=4, label=c)
ax.text(2025.2, d8_rate.loc[2025, "Fourth quarter"], pct(d8_rate.loc[2025, "Fourth quarter"]),
        fontsize=7.5, color=style.SERIES[0], va="center", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(2015.6, 2025.9)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.65)
ax.set_xticks(range(2016, 2026))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_ylabel("Went for two at down 8")
ax.set_title("Down 8 after the touchdown: from never to half the time")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
plt.show()
```

## Timeouts: pricing the clock

The third decision in this chapter's title is the quietest. [The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth
Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) showed what a timeout buys: a stop
of the clock that saves 30 to 40 seconds when the other team wants it running. What is that worth in
wins? Our random-walk model can't say (it doesn't know timeouts exist), but nflverse's model can, because
timeouts are among its inputs. Take every snap in the last 1:00-2:30 of a one-score game and ask how
nflverse's win probability moves with each team's timeouts, holding the score, field position, down,
distance and clock fixed with a regression.

```{python}
#| label: timeouts
lt = reg[(reg.qtr == 4) & reg.game_seconds_remaining.between(60, 150) & reg.down.notna()
         & reg.score_differential.between(-8, 8) & reg.wp.notna()]
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(lt)), lt.posteam_timeouts_remaining, lt.defteam_timeouts_remaining,
                     lt.score_differential, lt.yardline_100, lt.game_seconds_remaining,
                     lt.down, lt.ydstogo])
coef_to = np.linalg.lstsq(X, lt.wp.to_numpy(), rcond=None)[0]
print(f"{len(lt):,} snaps; nflverse WP per timeout: offense's own {100 * coef_to[1]:+.1f} pts, "
      f"defense's {100 * coef_to[2]:+.1f} pts")
```

In the last two minutes of a one-score game, each timeout in the offense's pocket is worth about
`{python} f"{100 * coef_to[1]:.1f}"` points of win probability to it in nflverse's model, and each of the
defense's about `{python} f"{100 * -coef_to[2]:.1f}"` points against it (a straight-line average over many
different situations; for a team trailing by a field goal at its own 25, the value is larger). Those are
modest numbers, and they explain two habits analysts criticise. **Burning a timeout early** to avoid a
delay of game, or to think about a fourth down, costs about a point of win probability that will be badly
missed later; it is often worth taking the 5-yard penalty instead. And **finishing a close loss with
timeouts unused** is pure waste: a timeout's whole value is in being spent.

The most theatrical timeout has the weakest case. **Icing the kicker** means calling a timeout just before
the opponent's late field-goal try, hoping the wait unsettles him.

```{python}
#| label: icing
fgl = reg.sort_values(["game_id", "play_id"])
prev_def_to = (fgl.timeout.shift(1).eq(1) & (fgl.timeout_team.shift(1) == fgl.defteam))
late_fg = fgl[(fgl.play_type == "field_goal") & (fgl.qtr == 4) & (fgl.game_seconds_remaining <= 120)].copy()
late_fg["iced"] = np.where(prev_def_to.loc[late_fg.index], "Iced (defense's timeout just before)",
                           "Not iced")
late_fg["made"] = (late_fg.field_goal_result == "made").astype(float)
late_fg["expected"] = p_fg(late_fg.kick_distance)
ice = late_fg.groupby("iced").agg(kicks=("made", "size"), made=("made", "mean"),
                                  expected=("expected", "mean"), distance=("kick_distance", "mean"))
ice["made - expected"] = ice.made - ice.expected
ice_se = np.sqrt(0.2 * 0.8 / ice.loc[ice.index.str.startswith("Iced"), "kicks"].iloc[0])
md_table(ice.assign(made=100 * ice.made, expected=100 * ice.expected,
                    **{"made - expected": 100 * ice["made - expected"]})
         .rename(columns={"made": "made (%)", "expected": "expected (%)",
                          "made - expected": "made - expected (pts)"}).reset_index()
         .rename(columns={"iced": "last-2-minute field goals, 2016-2025"}),
         widths=[24, 6, 7, 8, 7, 9])
```

Iced kicks were made about `{python} f"{-100 * ice.iloc[0]['made - expected']:.0f}"` points less often
than their distance predicts. But un-iced kicks in the same last two minutes also fell short, by about
`{python} f"{-100 * ice.iloc[1]['made - expected']:.0f}"` points (pressure, weather and bad spots are part
of every late kick), so icing's own effect is the difference, a couple of points, and with fewer than 200
iced kicks the uncertainty (a standard error of about `{python} f"{100 * ice_se:.0f}"` points) is larger
than that. Earlier studies reached the same verdict: no reliable evidence that icing works, and a real
cost, because the timeout might have been worth more saved for the next possession.[^icing] This is the
pattern of the whole chapter in miniature: a tradition that feels powerful, a data set that can't
confirm it, and a model that prices what the tradition costs.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Be the bot.** Make every fourth-down call live, before the offense decides, then check it against a
model afterwards.

- **Before the snap on fourth down, find the break-even rate in your head.** Short yardage between the
  20s: you need to convert about half the time, and league-average offenses convert fourth-and-1 about
  two times in three and fourth-and-2 a bit under 60%. Near the goal line the bar drops into the 20s or
  30s. In the opponent's 30-40 (the go zone), almost anything up to fourth-and-4 or 5 says go.
- **Then adjust for the score and clock.** Leading late: kicks gain value. Trailing late: kicks lose it,
  especially a field goal that doesn't tie.
- **Then adjust for the teams.** A great offense or a weak defense raises *this* play's conversion
  chance; a strong kicker makes the 50-yarder more attractive. This is the part the bot can't do.
- **Make your call, and say how close it is.** "Go, easily" or "toss-up, lean go." The size matters
  more than the sign.
- **After a touchdown when down 14**, say "go for two" before the extra-point unit runs on, and watch
  whether the coach agrees (about half do now).
- **Watch the broadcast win-probability bar on the big plays** and estimate the WPA: which play of the
  drive moved it most, and was it a scoring play or a high-leverage third down?
- **Afterwards**, look the decision up: the nfl4th calculator, a team's analytics account, or the code
  in this chapter (`decide(lead, yardline_100, yards_to_go, minutes_left)`). Log your calls in your
  prediction log with the model's gain; [Film Study and
  Charting](../15-capstone/15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) shows how to score your calibration.
:::

## Predict the play

The pictures use the course's position letters: on offense X, Z and H are wide receivers, Y and U tight
ends, F the fullback and T or R the running back; on defense E is an end, T a tackle, N a nose tackle,
S, M and W the strong-side, middle and weak-side linebackers, C a cornerback, \$ the nickel back, and FS
and SS the safeties.

```{python}
#| label: drill-helpers
from gridiron import Play, offense, defense


def situation(off, dfn, los, to_go, title, lateral=(-16, 16), window=None, width_in=5.6, notes=()):
    """A pre-snap picture with the line to gain in yellow."""
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=los, to_go=to_go, title=title)
    for text, at in notes:
        p.note(text, at=at)
    p.draw(lateral=lateral, window=window, width_in=width_in)
    plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Fourth-and-1 at your own 34, first quarter, 0-0.** The offense stays on the field in a two-back
I-formation; the defense brings its base 4-3 with the strong safety down, eight in the box. Should the
offense go for it or punt? What is the break-even conversion rate, and what did NFL teams actually do
here a decade ago and in 2025?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-own34
#| fig-cap: "Fourth-and-1 at the offense's own 34, first quarter, tied: 21 personnel in an I-formation (fullback and tailback behind the quarterback, one tight end) against a base 4-3 Under front with the strong safety rolled into the box and both corners pressed. The yellow line to gain is one yard away."
off = offense("i_form")
dfn = [q.moved(d=1.5) if q.pos == "CB" else q            # short yardage: corners press
       for q in defense("4-3_under", "single_high", off)]
situation(off, dfn, los=44, to_go=1, title="4th & 1, own 34, 1st quarter, 0-0",
          lateral=(-17, 17), window=(-9, 15))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
```{python}
#| label: drill-own34-answer
dr1 = decide(0, 66, 1, 52).iloc[0]
zone = reg[(reg.down == 4) & reg.play_type.isin(["pass", "run", "punt", "field_goal"])
           & (reg.ydstogo == 1) & reg.yardline_100.between(60, 70) & (reg.qtr <= 3)
           & reg.wp.between(0.3, 0.7)]
went = zone.groupby("season").play_type.apply(lambda s: s.isin(["pass", "run"]).mean())
print(f"Go {dr1.go:.1%} vs punt {dr1.punt:.1%}: gain {100 * dr1.gain:+.1f} pts; "
      f"break-even {dr1.breakeven:.0%}; P(convert) {dr1.p_conv:.0%}")
print(f"Teams went for it on 4th & 1 at their own 30-40 (Q1-3, close games): "
      f"{went.loc[2016]:.0%} in 2016, {went.loc[2025]:.0%} in 2025 ({len(zone)} fourth downs)")
```

**Go.** The break-even rate is just under 50%, and a league-average offense converts fourth-and-1 about
two times in three; with a quarterback sneak or a
[tush push](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tush-push) available, more. Failure hands the opponent the
ball at your 34, which hurts, but a punt from here only moves the ball about 40 yards, and the
conversion keeps a drive alive with three more downs. The gain of about three points of win probability
is one of the largest routine edges on the fourth-down map.

And the behaviour change is dramatic: in 2016, teams in close games went for it on fourth-and-1 at their
own 30 to 40 about `{python} pct(went.loc[2016])` of the time; in 2025, about
`{python} pct(went.loc[2025])`. The eight-man box doesn't change the answer much. It makes the run a
little harder and the play-action pass a little easier, which is a reason to pick the play carefully,
not a reason to punt.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Fourth-and-3 at the opponent's 8, fourth quarter, 6:30 left. You trail 21-17.** The offense lines up
in a three-receiver set, and the defense is in nickel with everyone within about 8 yards of the line, as
it must be this close to the end zone. Kick the 26-yard field goal to make it 21-20, or go for it? How
does the answer differ from the same fourth down in a tied first quarter?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-red
#| fig-cap: "Fourth-and-3 at the opponent's 8, trailing by 4 with 6:30 left: 11 personnel in a 3x1 shotgun trips set against a nickel defense with both safeties near the goal line and the end zone behind them. The yellow line to gain is at the 5."
off = [q.moved(w=-17.5) if q.key == "X" else q for q in offense("gun_trips")]
dfn = []
for q in defense("nickel", "two_high", off):
    if q.key in ("FS", "SS"):
        q = q.moved(d=8.0)                              # end line is 18 yards from the LOS
    elif q.pos == "CB":
        q = q.moved(d=4.0)
    dfn.append(q)
situation(off, dfn, los=102, to_go=3, title="4th & 3 at the 8, down 21-17, 6:30 left",
          lateral=(-20, 20), window=(-8, 18))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
```{python}
#| label: drill-red-answer
late_r = decide(-4, 8, 3, 6.5).iloc[0]
early_r = decide(0, 8, 3, 55).iloc[0]
print(f"Down 4, 6:30 left: go {late_r.go:.1%}, FG {late_r.fg:.1%} -> gain {100 * late_r.gain:+.1f} "
      f"pts, break-even {late_r.breakeven:.0%}")
print(f"Tied, Q1:         go {early_r.go:.1%}, FG {early_r.fg:.1%} -> gain {100 * early_r.gain:+.1f} "
      f"pts, break-even {early_r.breakeven:.0%}")
```

**Go, clearly.** The field goal is nearly automatic, but it leaves you trailing 21-20 and kicking off with
six minutes left, still needing more points. A conversion leaves first-and-goal inside the 5, where a
touchdown is likely and puts you ahead; a failure leaves the opponent backed up at its own 8, so even the
bad branch keeps you in the game. The break-even conversion rate is around `{python} pct(late_r.breakeven)`,
far below the roughly 50% that teams convert on fourth-and-3.

The same fourth down in a tied first quarter is still a go, but by about `{python} f"{100 * early_r.gain:.0f}"` points
instead of `{python} f"{100 * late_r.gain:.0f}"`: early, three points are worth about their face value, and a
near-certain field goal is a decent result. Late and behind,
the field goal's three points are worth much less than three, because they don't change what you still
need. That difference, between points and wins, is the whole reason this chapter exists.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**You trailed 22-8, and with 9:00 left in the fourth quarter you have just scored a touchdown: it is
22-14.** The offense stays on the field at the 2. Kick the extra point (down 7) or go
for two (down 6 if it works, still down 8 if it doesn't)? What do teams do now?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-two
#| fig-cap: "The try after a touchdown, snapped from the 2: an 11-personnel shotgun 2x2 set against a nickel defense squeezed into the end zone (the end line is 12 yards behind the line of scrimmage). The yellow line is the goal line."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = []
for q in defense("nickel", "two_high", off):
    if q.key in ("FS", "SS"):
        q = q.moved(d=6.5, w=np.sign(q.w) * 6.0)        # inside the slots, deep in the end zone
    elif q.pos in ("CB", "NB"):
        q = q.moved(d=2.0)                              # tight on the receivers
    dfn.append(q)
situation(off, dfn, los=108, to_go=2, title="Down 8 after the TD, 9:00 left: kick or go?",
          lateral=(-17, 17), window=(-8, 12))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Go for two.** This is the down-14 problem: you were down 14 (22-8), you scored, and you are down 8 before
the try. Using the tree from this chapter with the league's 2016-2025 rates, going for two now wins about
`{python} pct(w_go_first(P2))` of the games in which you score the next touchdown and stop the opponent,
against `{python} pct(w_kick_first(P2))` for kicking, and it is better whenever your two-point play
succeeds more than about `{python} pct(breakeven_p)` of the time. If the try fails, you know with nine
minutes left that you need a touchdown and a two-pointer, and you can manage fourth downs and timeouts
accordingly.

What do teams do? In 2016 and 2017 nobody in this spot went for two. In 2025, about
`{python} pct(d8_rate.loc[2025, "Fourth quarter"])` of fourth-quarter tries at down 8 were two-point
attempts: the fastest-moving decision in this chapter, and a sign that when a decision is a single
clean tree, coaches adopt the math quickly.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Win probability is a model of the rest of the game.** A random walk of points, scaled by
  √(time left) and started from the lead plus the possession's expected points, matches nflverse's
  machine-learning model on 2025 data; the betting line adds what both lack, which team is better.
  Check a model by its calibration, not by one game: 99% means one collapse in a hundred, and Super Bowl
  LI was one.
- **WPA scores plays by how much they changed the chance of winning**, and leverage says how much a
  situation lets a play matter. A tenth of plays carry about two-fifths of all win-probability movement;
  most of the game is setting up the few snaps that decide it.
- **A fourth-down decision is a probability tree.** Conversion probability times the win probability of
  each outcome, against the field goal and the punt. The break-even conversion rate is the one number to
  carry: go if you believe the play converts more often than that.
- **The map says go on short yardage almost everywhere**, go in the opponent's 30-40, and punt on long
  yardage in your own half; the score and clock then shift it: kicks gain value when leading late and
  lose it when trailing.
- **Respect the model's limits.** Simple models break in the last five minutes, where scoring is lumpy and
  the clock is controllable. Every model assumes average teams, and models disagree by a point or more on
  close calls. Read the size of the gain, not just its sign.
- **Coaches moved toward the math, partly.** On clear-go fourth downs the go rate doubled from 2016 to
  2025 but stayed under half; the down-14 two-point decision went from never to about half of
  fourth-quarter tries. Detroit followed the model more often than any other team.
